vignette:
He is a 66-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working as a roofer, a job he describes with a mixture of pride and fatigue. He is married, and his wife is one of the few people with whom he feels fully understood, though he still tries hard not to burden her. For years he has worked with his body rather than his words, rising before dawn, carrying bundles of shingles up ladders, and measuring a day's success by whether a roof is sealed before the weather changes. He has always seen himself as someone who can endure discomfort without complaint.

The event that changed that came not during a dramatic accident, but during a workday that began like many others. He is on a roof when he notices a sharp chemical smell drifting across the site. At first he assumes it is solvent, something he can tolerate until the job is done. But the odor grows stronger, and then there is a burning in his nose and throat, followed by coughing that does not stop. His eyes water so badly that the roofline blurs. He remembers feeling trapped by the heat, the height, and the realization that something in the air is making it hard to breathe. He climbs down with shaking legs, embarrassed by how suddenly his body seems to fail him. By the time he gets home, he feels dizzy, sick to his stomach, and frightened in a way that is hard for him to admit, even to himself.

In the days that follow, he expects the discomfort to pass. Instead, his body remains on alert. He wakes before dawn with his heart racing, already tense, as though he is back on the job site and the smell is in the air again. He starts noticing chemical odors everywhere-in cleaning products, gasoline, fresh paint, even in the rubber smell of a new tool bag. A faint scent can make his chest tighten and his mind jump immediately to the roof, the coughing, the helplessness of being unable to escape quickly enough. He begins avoiding places where the air feels enclosed or "wrong," standing near doors in stores and keeping windows open in the car even when the weather is cold. He will not enter a building if he thinks there has been recent work done with chemicals, and he becomes especially uneasy around paint thinner or adhesive fumes. What others dismiss as a harmless smell can send him into a full day of unease.

He is still working, but the job no longer feels straightforward. As a roofer, he is used to high places, heat, and hard labor, yet now he becomes preoccupied with what might be on the materials, whether something has been treated, whether a surface smell means danger. He checks and rechecks instructions, sometimes taking longer than necessary because he cannot let himself move on until he feels certain. He notices that he is more irritable with coworkers and more easily startled by sudden movement or loud equipment noise. If a truck backfires or a can lid snaps open with a sharp hiss, his body jerks before he can think. He hates that this happens in front of others, because it feels like weakness.

At home, he is quieter than he used to be. He still sits with his wife in the evenings, but he often seems far away, staring at the television without following it. He does not like talking about the exposure, partly because he does not want sympathy and partly because the memory feels easier to contain when left unspoken. Yet when he does speak, he returns to the same details: the smell, the burning, the fear that his lungs would close. His sleep is shallow and broken, and he sometimes lies awake replaying the day in fragments, wondering whether he should have left sooner, whether he should have known better, whether something inside him was permanently changed. He feels embarrassed by how much the memory lingers, especially because he has survived so many other physical demands over the years.

He presents now as a man who still performs competence, but with more effort and less ease. He remains loyal to his work, his family, and the identity he has built through endurance, yet a part of him is now watching the air, watching his body, and watching for the next moment when something ordinary might suddenly feel dangerous.
